## Question

An optimiser's stopping test needs the derivative of f(x) = exp(x) sin(x)
on the interval from 0.5{claim:x_lo} to 1.0{claim:x_hi}, at
101{claim:npoints} equally spaced points, each with a relative error below
1e-12{claim:target}. Can central differences with the usual step deliver
that, or are dual numbers needed? The quantity of interest is the largest
relative error of f' over the points, for each method. Only its order of
magnitude matters: the answer is which method to use.

## Scales and estimate

The interval and f are of order 1, and so are f' and f''' on it, so the
error model of a central difference needs no other scale: truncation
h^2 |f'''| / 6 and rounding about eps |f| / h. Balancing the two gives a
step near eps^(1/3), about 6e-6, and an error near eps^(2/3), about 4e-11.
My estimate of the best error was 4e-11{estimate:cd_err}. That is above
the budget, so I expected central differences to fail.

## Model and assumptions

Float64 arithmetic with correctly rounded elementary functions. The ground
truth is the exact derivative evaluated in 256-bit BigFloat at each Float64
point, whose own error is negligible. Errors are relative to |f'|, which
has no zero on the interval (sin x + cos x > 1 there); near a zero of f'
every relative error would grow without bound and the comparison would
mean nothing.

## Method choice

At the rule step cbrt(eps) max(1, |x|), which is
6.06e-6{claim:rule_step} on this interval, central differences reach a
largest relative error of 1.66e-11{claim:cd_err} over the points, and a
smallest of 4.6e-13{claim:cd_err_min}; dual numbers reach
2.2e-16{claim:dual_err}. Central differences miss the budget by more than
a factor of ten at every step tried (see Verification), so the choice is
dual{claim:choice}.

For a gradient the costs are also counted: 5{claim:grad_evals_dual}
evaluations of f on duals for 5 variables by forward mode, against
10{claim:grad_evals_central} evaluations on floats by central differences.
A dual evaluation does more arithmetic than a float one, so the counts do
not say which is faster in seconds.

## Verification

The dual numbers are exact where the arithmetic is: on a degree-5
polynomial with small integer coefficients at the dyadic point 0.75 the
derivative's error is 0{claim:poly_err}. A second derivative by nested
duals has a relative error of 1.1e-16{claim:nested_err}, and a 5-variable
gradient 5.0e-17{claim:grad_err}.

The central difference behaves as its error model says. At x = 0.7 the
fitted slope of log error on log h is 1.996{claim:trunc_order} for steps
from 0.0039{claim:trunc_fit_hmin} to 0.125{claim:trunc_fit_hmax}, where
truncation dominates (theory 2), and -1.02{claim:round_slope} for steps
from 2.84e-14{claim:round_fit_hmin} to 9.31e-10{claim:round_fit_hmax},
where rounding dominates (theory -1).

The best uniform step on a quarter-octave grid, the one with the smallest
largest error over all 101 points, is 7.63e-6{claim:cd_best_h}; the model's
optimum at the middle of the interval is 1.66e-5{claim:cd_theory_h}, a
factor of 2.2 away. At the best step the largest error is
1.19e-11{claim:cd_best_err}: no step does much better than the rule.

## Validation

Dual numbers give the derivative of the code, which is the derivative
wanted only if the code computes the function wanted. Three Newton steps
for sqrt(2) from 1 give the value with a relative error of
1.5e-6{claim:algo_value_err}, and the dual derivative of those three steps
is off from 1 / (2 sqrt 2) by 3.5e-5{claim:algo_deriv_err}: the derivative
of an unconverged iteration is less accurate than its value. After
5{claim:algo_iters} steps both are at rounding level.

## Uncertainty and sensitivity

Over the points the central difference's error at the rule step spreads
from 4.6e-13 to 1.66e-11 (Method choice): single points can look good by
cancellation, and the largest error is the honest number.

The perturbed assumption: the same interval moved by 96 pi, from
302.09{claim:robust_x_lo} to 302.59{claim:robust_x_hi}. The function has
the same shape there, but the rule makes the step 300 times larger, and
central differences reach a largest error of 3.3e-7{claim:robust_cd_err}.
Dual numbers stay at 2.2e-16{claim:robust_dual_err}, so the choice is
still dual{claim:robust_choice}, and the conclusion holds{claim:robust_holds}.
The rule fails because it assumes f varies on the scale of |x|, which
exp(x) sin(x) does not.

## Claims and limits

For this function and budget, central differences cannot deliver twelve
digits at any step, and dual numbers deliver them with four orders of
magnitude to spare. This was tested for x from 0.5{claim:valid_x_min} to
302.59{claim:valid_x_max}, on two intervals, and is claimed nowhere else:
not for other functions, not for intervals containing a zero of f', not
for cost in seconds, and not for many inputs, where forward mode's one
pass per input becomes the cost that matters.
